name: Essential Products
oneLiner: A premium Android phone startup from Android's co-creator, with a titanium body, edge-to-edge screen and snap-on accessories.
causeOfDeath: Its only phone shipped late with a weak camera into a market owned by Apple and Samsung; sales disappointed, the founder was mired in scandal, and cash ran out.
moneyNote: Reported $300M round (Amazon, Tencent, Foxconn among investors) and a valuation of over $1B in 2017, per reports cited by Wikipedia. No sale; the company closed in 2020.
inOneMinute: Andy Rubin, **the man who co-created Android**, launched Essential to build a better phone. Investors reportedly valued it at **over $1 billion** before it shipped.
The $699 Essential Phone arrived late, with **a disappointing camera**. Within two months, the price was cut to $499 because of low demand.
Rubin's past at Google became headline news. The next phone was cancelled, and in February 2020 **Essential shut down**, ending updates overnight.
killerLine: A famous founder can raise money, but **only the product can win customers**. In phones, that means a great camera and a reason to switch.

chapters.title: The idea: Android's father builds a phone
chapters.body: Andy Rubin co-created Android, the software that runs most of the world's phones. After leaving Google, he founded Essential Products in November 2015, backed by his own startup studio, Playground Global. The plan was bold: build **a premium phone free of clutter**, with a titanium body, a screen stretching almost to the edges, and magnetic connectors for snap-on accessories. In May 2017 he unveiled the Essential Phone and a smart-home speaker. Investors including Amazon, Tencent and Foxconn reportedly put in $300 million, and by August 2017 the company was reported to be worth **over $1 billion**, before it had sold a single phone.

chapters.title: The rise: a beautiful launch, slightly late
chapters.body: After missing its shipping dates, the Essential Phone went on sale on **17 August 2017 for $699**, with Sprint as its exclusive US carrier. Reviewers loved the design, the speed and the clean version of Android. It even worked on other US networks, not just Sprint. But the camera was a real weakness. Engadget found early low-light photos grainy and blurry, with lag when switching lenses, even after two quick software fixes. Its verdict: **"camera buffs should look elsewhere."** At a price close to an iPhone or a Galaxy, a weak camera was a serious problem.

chapters.title: The cracks: low sales and a scandal
chapters.body: Sales were weak. In October 2017, just two months after launch, Essential **cut the price to $499** because of low demand, giving earlier buyers a $200 code. In November 2017 the tech publication The Information reported that Rubin had left Google in 2014 after an investigation into a relationship with a woman who worked in Android. Rubin took a leave of absence from Essential, saying he needed to deal with personal matters, and returned in December. In October 2018, The New York Times reported that Google had found a misconduct claim against him credible and still paid him a **$90 million exit package**. Rubin called the reports false. Either way, the story damaged trust in the company's leader.

chapters.title: The fall: no clear path
chapters.body: In May 2018 Essential cancelled its next flagship phone and was reported to be looking for a buyer. The original phone was discontinued in December 2018. Essential bought the email app company CloudMagic (maker of Newton Mail) and in October 2019 teased **Project Gem**, a tall, narrow phone with a new interface. But the money was running low. On 12 February 2020, Essential announced it was shutting down immediately, saying there was **no clear path to deliver Gem to customers**. The Essential Phone stopped getting software and security updates. Newton Mail closed in April. In just over four years, a reported billion-dollar company had disappeared.

mistakes.title: Took on Apple and Samsung with one phone
mistakes.explain: Essential's first and only phone was priced at $699, right against the iPhone and Galaxy. Those giants have huge marketing budgets, store shelves and loyal users. **A newcomer needs a big reason for people to switch**, and Essential's clean design and Android experience were not enough on their own.

mistakes.title: Shipped with a weak camera
mistakes.explain: For most buyers, the camera is the most important part of a phone. Essential's was poor in low light, slow to switch lenses and basic in features. **Reviewers' first impressions stuck**, even after software fixes. Launching a flagship before its most important feature is ready can sink it.

mistakes.title: Founder controversy at the top
mistakes.explain: Reports about Rubin's exit from Google forced him to take leave just three months after launch, and the 2018 New York Times story drew global attention. Rubin denied wrongdoing. Still, **when the founder is the brand, his reputation is the company's reputation**, and buyers, staff and partners notice.

mistakes.title: Valued at $1 billion before proving demand
mistakes.explain: Essential was reported to be a unicorn before it sold a single phone. That raised expectations that no first product could easily meet. Within two months, **the price was cut by $200**, a clear sign demand was well below plan.

mistakes.title: Hard-to-repair premium hardware
mistakes.explain: iFixit gave the phone **1 out of 10 for repairability**: heavy glue, no visible screws, and a screen that broke when removed. Premium materials raise costs and make repairs expensive, which hurts both margins and customer goodwill after sale. Customers notice when a small crack means a big bill.

warningSigns: Is your launch price the same as the market leader's while your product is weaker in the feature buyers care about most?
Have you missed your shipping date and still not fixed the main complaint from testers?
Did you have to cut prices within weeks of launch?
Would a scandal about one founder be enough to damage your whole company's brand?
Is your valuation based on the founder's fame rather than on sales?

lessons.title: Find the feature buyers care about most and nail it
lessons.detail: For phones it's the camera; for a food app it may be delivery time. Ask 20 target customers what decides their purchase, and don't launch until that part is excellent.

lessons.title: Don't attack giants head-on
lessons.detail: Start in a niche the giants ignore, like a specific price band, region or user group, then expand. Ask: which customers do the big brands serve badly?

lessons.title: Fame opens doors, not wallets
lessons.detail: A famous founder makes fundraising and press easy. Customers still judge only the product in their hand.

lessons.title: Founder conduct is a business risk
lessons.detail: Investors, staff and customers now treat leadership behaviour as part of a company's value. Set clear workplace rules from day one, including for founders.

lessons.title: Plan for your customers if you shut down
lessons.detail: Essential stopped phone updates the day it closed. If you sell devices, promise and fund a minimum support period so buyers are not left exposed.

afterlife.text: Essential closed in February 2020 and Newton Mail shut that April. Andy Rubin had quietly left Playground Global in 2019 and has denied the misconduct allegations. In February 2021, Carl Pei, co-founder of OnePlus, bought the Essential brand for his new company Nothing.

disputed.claim: How many Essential Phones were sold
disputed.note: Reports range from about 5,000 through Sprint in the first month, to Essential's claim of six-figure sales, to a Bloomberg estimate of about 150,000. None was confirmed.
Reported by The Information and The New York Times; Rubin denied them, calling them false and part of a smear campaign. Not proven in court.
The $300M round and $1B+ valuation come from press reports; Essential never published audited figures.
